units.translation: b. στυγερόν means both 'hated' and 'fearful'; here perhaps 'toilsome'.

246-47a. ἦ ῥα θεοὺς ὀλο〈ῇσιν〉: 'Have you then acted impiously toward the gods and erred by some wickedness?' Or 'by paths', that is, having turned aside from the straight and just way; from ἀτραπός, which means 'path'.
b. ἀφραδίῃσι: written ἀτροπίῃσι in Lg and P.
c. 〈μαντοσύνας δεδαώς:〉 instead of 'prophesying against the will of the gods'.
d. δεδαώς means 'having learned' rather than 'teaching'. For because you learned, he says, the art of prophecy and prophesied against the will of the gods, you sinned against the gods.

b. εἰ δὴ πρόχνυ γέ〈ρας〉: if indeed the divinity has entrusted this honor to us, so as to help you. The sentence is in hyperbaton, so that it would be thus: 'but the mind within us is frightened, eager as we are to help; for conspicuous to mortals are the reproaches of the immortals, if indeed the divinity has granted this privilege utterly.'
c. But we, if we truly have the privilege from the divinity, fear lest the divine be angry.
e. ἀρίζηλοι: the punishments of the gods are very conspicuous and clear.

b. θεοῖς ἀπὸ θυμοῦ ἔσεσθαι: for that helping the impious involves impiety toward the gods, Euripides also says (Or. 534 sq.): 'So that you may know, Menelaus, do not act contrary to the gods, wishing to help this man.' For Orestes seems to him to be impious.

257. ἴστω Λητοῦς υἱός: he has taken the oath from the poet (A 86): 'for by Apollo, dear to Zeus'. For it was fitting for a seer who was bringing someone to trust to swear by the god who is the patron of his art.

259a. καὶ τόδ’ ἐπ’ ὀφθαλμῶν ὀλοὸν νέφος: written also ἀλαόν. Some accuse Apollonius of not having introduced this oath well; for he swears by things by which he cannot be harmed. But it must be said that the oath becomes more impassioned when one swears by one's own misfortune (υ 339): 'No by Zeus, Agelaus, and by the sorrows of my father'. And Demosthenes (De cor. 208): 'by those who risked their lives at Marathon and those who fought at Plataea'. It was an ancient custom, first to swear by the gods, then to add also one's own misfortunes.
b. καὶ τόδ’ ἐπ’ ὀφθ〈αλμῶν〉 ἀλαὸν νέφος: [he says:] the blind cloud and the mist that lies upon me. It is customary to swear by one's own misfortunes.
260. οἳ μηδ’ οἵδε: who not even these may be well-disposed to him as a perjurer. From the Homeric (Τ 264): 'but if any of these things is falsely sworn, may the gods give me sorrows'.
263a. κουρότεροι: the comparative is used instead of the positive.
